extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students studying real analysis / rigorous calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and main theorems for the Riemann integral in one variable: partitions, upper/lower sums, integrability tests, operations on integrals, limit-interchange conditions, fundamental theorem of calculus, change of variables, and related results (including complex-valued functions and Taylor remainder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition and mesh definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition P of [a,b] is a subdivision x0 ≤ x1 ≤ ··· ≤ xn with xi in [a,b]; equal consecutive points are permitted and the multiplicity of xj is the number of times it occurs. The mesh µ(P) = max_i (xi − xi−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partitions allowing equal points permit integration over zero-length intervals. Multiplicities must be preserved in refinements. Use µ(P) to control uniform continuity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper and lower sums and extremal values on subintervals
rubrics_metrics.description: For each subinterval [x_{i-1},x_i] let Mi = sup_{x in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x) and mi = inf_{x in [x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x). Define U(P,f)=Σ Mi·(x_i−x_{i-1}) and L(P,f)=Σ mi·(x_i−x_{i-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper sums and lower sums visualize as sums of rectangle areas: upper sums use smallest rectangles whose heights are just sufficient to lie above f; lower sums use largest rectangles lying below the graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper and lower Riemann integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: The upper Riemann integral is inf_{partitions P} U(P,f) and the lower Riemann integral is sup_{partitions P} L(P,f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These extremal values bracket any candidate integral; equality of the two defines Riemann integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Riemann integrability
rubrics_metrics.description: f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] if the upper and lower Riemann integrals are equal; in that case their common value is denoted ∫_a^b f dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (Lemma 1.25(e)): f is integrable iff for each ε>0 there exists a partition P with U(P,f) − L(P,f) < ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and basic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant functions integrate to area c(b−a). The Dirichlet-type function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is discontinuous everywhere and yields U(P,f)=1 and L(P,f)=0 for every partition, hence is not Riemann integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that discontinuity at every point can prevent integrability, while boundedness and limited discontinuities often permit integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound inequalities for integrals (Lemma 1.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If m ≤ f(x) ≤ M on [a,b] then m(b−a) ≤ L(P,f) ≤ ∫_a^b f dx ≤ U(P,f) ≤ M(b−a); taking sup/inf over partitions yields m(b−a) ≤ lower integral ≤ upper integral ≤ M(b−a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bounds give crude control on the integral and are useful in convergence and comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement monotonicity (Lemma 1.25 parts a–c)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P* refines P then L(P,f) ≤ L(P*,f) and U(P*,f) ≤ U(P,f). For any partitions P1,P2 a common refinement P* satisfies L(P1,f) ≤ L(P*,f) ≤ U(P*,f) ≤ U(P2,f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refinements can only increase lower sums and decrease upper sums; use common refinements to compare sums from different partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability equivalent partition criterion (Lemma 1.25(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] iff for each ε>0 there exists a partition P with U(P,f) − L(P,f) < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard constructive test for integrability; it is used repeatedly in proofs (choose P to make upper and lower sums arbitrarily close).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity implies Riemann integrability (Theorem 1.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] (hence uniformly continuous) then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity to make Mi−mi small on each subinterval by choosing partition mesh < δ, then Lemma 1.25(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity over adjacent intervals (Lemma 1.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: If c in [a,b], then f is integrable on [a,b] iff it is integrable on [a,c] and [c,b], and in that case ∫_a^b f = ∫_a^c f + ∫_c^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for reducing global integrability to integrability on smaller intervals; proof uses unions of partitions and refinement arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-to-global integrability near isolated points (Lemma 1.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] and for each δ>0 f is Riemann integrable on all closed subintervals contained in [a,b] that stay at least δ away from a given point c, then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma allows handling finitely many bad points by excluding arbitrarily small neighborhoods around them and patching using Lemma 1.27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite discontinuities suffice (Proposition 1.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] and is continuous except at finitely many points, then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No restriction to jump discontinuities; any finite set of discontinuities is allowed. Proof by induction using Lemmas 1.27 and 1.28.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of the integral (Proposition 1.30(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 and f2 are Riemann integrable on [a,b], then f1+f2 and c·f are integrable and ∫(f1+f2)=∫f1+∫f2, ∫(c f)=c ∫f for any real c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses inequalities comparing L and U sums for sums and scalar multiples and Lemma 1.25(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and comparison properties (Proposition 1.30(c),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 ≤ f2 on [a,b] then ∫_a^b f1 ≤ ∫_a^b f2. If m ≤ f ≤ M then m(b−a) ≤ ∫_a^b f ≤ M(b−a). Also |∫ f| ≤ ∫ |f|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties follow from comparing supremum/infimum on subintervals and the integrability of absolute values (via continuous composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability preserved under continuous composition (Proposition 1.30(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with range contained in [m,M] and φ:[m,M]→R is continuous, then φ∘f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform continuity of φ on the compact range and partition control of f's oscillation; shows many nonlinear transforms preserve integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products, powers, and absolute values (Proposition 1.30(f),(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: If f1 and f2 are integrable then f1·f2 is integrable. If f is integrable then |f| and (f)^p (for integer p≥1) are integrable under appropriate boundedness conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic identities and earlier integrability-preserving results (composition, linearity) to deduce integrability of products and powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of naive limit-interchange without uniformity (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example fn(x)=n for 0<x<1/n and 0 otherwise: each fn is Riemann integrable with ∫_0^1 fn = 1, but fn(x)→0 for each fixed x, so pointwise limit is 0 with integral 0; interchange of limit and integral fails without additional hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that pointwise convergence is insufficient; motivates uniform convergence hypothesis (Theorem 1.31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence allows interchange of limit and integral (Theorem 1.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fn are Riemann integrable on [a,b] and converge uniformly to f on [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable and lim_{n→∞} ∫_a^b fn = ∫_a^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform Cauchy criterion and bounding by small uniform ε_n, together with linearity and integrability of constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Theorem 1.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If f is continuous on [a,b], then G(x)=∫_a^x f(t) dt is differentiable on (a,b) with G'(x)=f(x), and G is continuous at endpoints. (b) If F is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) with F'=f, then ∫_a^b f = F(b)−F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem connects differentiation and integration; (a) follows from Riemann integrability and continuity, (b) follows from the mean value theorem corollary applied to F−G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts (Corollary 1.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are continuously differentiable on [a,b], then ∫_a^b f(x) g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b − ∫_a^b f'(x) g(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from product rule and Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; requires continuous derivatives on closed interval (endpoints included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-variables formula (Theorem 1.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be Riemann integrable on [a,b]. Let φ:[A,B]→[a,b] be continuous, strictly increasing and onto, with continuous inverse φ^{-1} on [a,b], differentiable on (A,B) with uniformly continuous derivative φ'. Then (f∘φ)·φ' is Riemann integrable on [A,B] and ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_A^B f(φ(y)) φ'(y) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform continuity of φ' ensures boundedness; remarks note continuity of φ^{-1} can be automatic under stronger hypotheses but is assumed here for simplicity. Proof maps partitions via φ and uses Mean Value Theorem on subintervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sums convergence and converse (Theorem 1.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b], then for any choice of sample points t_i in subintervals of a partition P, S(P,f)=Σ f(t_i)·(x_i−x_{i-1}) → ∫_a^b f dx as µ(P)→0. Conversely, if there exists r such that for every ε>0 there is δ>0 with |S(P,f)−r|<ε whenever µ(P)<δ, then f is Riemann integrable and r=∫_a^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The direct part splits contributions by relation to a fixed fine partition; the converse reduces to upper/lower sum closeness via specially chosen sample points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrals of complex-valued functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ∫ f for complex-valued f by integrating real and imaginary parts: if f=u+iv with u,v real, then ∫ f = ∫ u + i ∫ v; f is integrable iff u and v are integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most properties for real-valued integrals carry over componentwise (linearity, bounds, convergence of Riemann sums). Some real-only facts (Mean Value Theorem) do not hold for complex-valued functions, but results are recovered by treating real and imaginary parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's Theorem with integral remainder (Theorem 1.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has n+1 continuous derivatives on the closed interval between a and x, then f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x−a)+...+ f^{(n)}(a)/n! (x−a)^n + R_n(a,x), where R_n(a,x) = (1/n!) ∫_a^x (x−t)^n f^{(n+1)}(t) dt (with appropriate sign/variant if x<a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remainder is written as an integral of the next derivative; proof proceeds by induction using integration by parts. Applies to complex-valued functions as well.
